selected_news.source_headline: High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31
selected_news.article_text: Simon Stiell makes opening address at summit in Turkey, where talks are under way about speeding up shift to electrification A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet, the UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, told the opening plenary of critical UN climate talks in Turkey Stiell joined Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an optimistic alternative to a planet still tied to oil, coal and gas Inside the tight security of the opening plenary on Monday, delegates from almost 200 countries watched a stirring short film with scenes of fire, flood and storms that proclaimed: “It’s time to reconnect with the planet we have grown apart from.” Turkey said it expected 100,000 visitors, including national delegations, to attend the two-week talks, including at least 95 heads of state. A global leaders summit is scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday. But the talks are under increased pressure to deliver, after growing dissatisfaction with the snail’s pace of results The talks are opening as a historic El Niño builds in the tropical Pacific and months after a glacier collapse set off catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet, wiping away villages and killing at least 1,459 people, with thousands more still missing. Climate scientists confirmed this year that global heating would reach at least 1.8C – beyond the 1.5C temperature goal that countries promised to aim for at talks in Paris in 2015 Last week Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told the Guardian that although he still had faith in the negotiating process, “the fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast … and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.” And in a statement the UN secretary general, António Guterres, urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need” Stiell also said: “The urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth,” adding that it was vulnerable communities paying the price and frustration at a lack of fairness was palpable US president Donald Trump’s war with Iran and the disruption of the key strait of Hormuz supply route for oil pushed up petrol prices around the world by 50%, raising inflation and slowing economic growth Stiell told delegates this “fossil fuel cost chaos” had “delivered a global shock wave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer” Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, the president of the negotiations, said in a speech that will set the tone for the talks that although the 1.5C Paris target will be overshot “we can return … if we work together and act with urgency, solidarity and resolve” With fists clenched in the final moments of a speech, Bowen urged delegates to show future generations that this generation was “equal to the challenge” and to “rise to this moment together” The countries pushing for the greatest action at Cop31 have stressed the 1.5C temperature rise limit can’t be abandoned and called for accelerated steps to provide finance to the places most vulnerable to climate impacts. The so-called high-ambition coalition said it has 20 country members pushing for major progress in Antalya. “That limit is in serious danger but overshoot should never become an excuse for inaction, every fraction of a degree matters,” said Jess Gasper, an environmental official for the Marshall Islands “We must limit overshoot and return to a safe temperature as quickly as possible.” Gasper said it took eight years to get international finance to build a single sea wall to help protect the Marshall Islands, a Pacific island nation acutely threatened by sea level rise “That example shows we need that money to adapt,” he said. “I refuse to accept that we experience displacement because the world fails to act.” The talks began without a fight over the agenda, which was considered by many to be a good sign. There was confidence among delegates that a final decision from Cop31 would include reference to a new voluntary electrification goal being championed by the host, Turkey, and the president of the negotiations, Australia Bowen said he had spoken to countries around the globe that were represented at the talks and there was “enormous momentum” among them for electrification The goal, he said, was to raise the percentage of final energy consumption coming from electricity from the current one-fifth to one-third in the next ten years Dr Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency, said: “I have talked with many governments and I see there is a great appetite for many countries to be part of this historic decision [in Antalya].” He told the Guardian: “The important thing is that we are entering the age of electricity and this [electrification goal] would give an extra boost to that movement.” Countries agreed at the 2023 climate summit to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030. Birol said if countries endorsed the 2035 electrification target it would give an “unmistakable signal to markets” and a chance to increase both renewable and nuclear electricity

selected_news.title: Aliaga’da Çelik Fabrikasında 17 Ölüyle Patlama
selected_news.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.
selected_news.source_headline: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people
selected_news.article_text: At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan originally said the death toll was 16, but the Health Minister, Kemal Memişoğlu, later announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died, taking the toll to 17 Eyewitnesses at the scene said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs Rock collapse kills two in Turkey's Cappadocia, local media reports Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says

selected_news.source_headline: Senate advances bill to speed up permit reviews for infrastructure projects
selected_news.article_text: Chamber voted 73-25 to formally take up bill that will shorten timelines to start energy and datacenter projects The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face years-long delays in getting to the grid The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started – both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects – and make sure datacenters pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence datacenters and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families”, Trump wrote Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals Midterm results could complicate bill’s passage in lame-duck sessions While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats’ sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy, but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of datacenters powered by natural gas Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting The bill’s four main champions – two Democrats and two Republicans – released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, a Republican senator of West Virginia, Mike Lee, a Republican senator of Utah, Martin Heinrich a Democratic senator of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator of Rhode Island, say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years “Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for datacenters instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, Heinrich said Capito called the bill “a win for America”, adding: “We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity … to come together to show the American people we are listening to you.”

selected_news.title: COP31 Antalya’da Açıldı: 90.000 Katılımla Kararlar
selected_news.summary: COP31 opens in Antalya: Can climate promises finally deliver results? UN News
selected_news.source_headline: COP31 opens in Antalya: Can climate promises finally deliver results?
selected_news.article_text: COP31 opens in Antalya: Can climate promises finally deliver results? Nearly 200 countries have arrived on Türkiye's Mediterranean coast for a climate summit with a different ambition: fewer grand declarations and more concrete decisions. With a powerful El Niño threatening to worsen extreme weather, negotiators face difficult questions over climate finance, clean energy and how to protect communities already living with the consequences of climate change. Today at COP31 - COP31 opens: More than 90,000 people are expected in Antalya as pressure mounts to deliver on climate promises. The summit is set to close on Friday, 20 November. - Australia seeks early deal: Countries are being asked to start shaping a political agreement from the outset, rather than waiting until the final days. - Finance remains a sticking point: Developing countries are pressing for faster access to climate finance, while clean energy, adaptation and a just transition top the agenda. - Focus on human impacts: Food, Agriculture and Health Day spotlights growing risks and practical solutions. The Mediterranean city of Antalya is no stranger to history. Greeks, Romans, Byzantines and Ottomans have all left their mark on this stretch of Türkiye’s southern coast. Now, as nearly 200 countries gather here for the latest UN climate summit, COP31, the question is whether they can add a new chapter of their own by turning decades of climate promises into action. Inside the vast conference venue, the Turkish tulip featured in the COP31 logo is a recurring sight as participants navigate long corridors leading to national pavilions and negotiating rooms. Beyond the bustle of the conference halls, the stakes are high. As extreme weather impacts mount worldwide, governments face growing pressure to show that decades of climate commitments can deliver results. “Progress is nowhere near far enough or fair enough,” UN Climate Change chief Simon Stiell told the opening plenary on Monday, urging countries to move beyond setting targets and “supercharge solutions” that can make a difference on the ground. “No COP is a silver bullet. No single conference can bridge the chasm between the science and reality,” he said. The test for negotiators Unlike summits dominated by a single landmark agreement, COP31 is focused on turning existing commitments into action. Türkiye’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum officially took the gavel this morning as the COP31 President, while Australia’s Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen will oversee negotiations under an unusual co-presidency arrangement agreed during COP30. “Our decisions must take shape in a city’s infrastructure, on a farmer’s land and along a factory's production line. Families must feel their impact in lower energy bills,” Mr. Kurum told delegates. Mr. Bowen announced plans to develop a presidency-led decision throughout the conference, rather than waiting until its final days. The aim is to agree on practical measures to accelerate climate action, although differences remain over how ambitious the outcome should be. Finance is expected to be the one of the toughest issues, with developing countries seeking faster access to funding for adaptation and cleaner development. Negotiators must also advance agreements on emissions reductions and a just transition. “We know there will be a difference of views – on the value of the decision, on its elements, on how far we go. But our job is to work to close those differences and provide the most ambitious, most outcome-orientated decision that consensus will allow,” Mr. Bowen explained. When climate change becomes a health emergency Monday was also Food, Agriculture and Health Day, bringing attention to the growing toll of climate change on human health. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), between 3.3 and 3.6 billion people live in areas highly vulnerable to climate change. Extreme heat, floods and shifting weather patterns are already putting lives at risk and straining health systems worldwide. “The main character at the center of this story is not the atmosphere. It's not the land, the ocean or the ice. It’s us. You and me, our family and our communities,” Alan Dangour of the Wellcome Trust Foundation said during a press conference by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), urging climate negotiators to put people at the heart of their decisions. “We cannot adapt to an unmitigated future,” Mr. Dangour warned. Extreme heat offers a particularly troubling example. Scientists are increasingly concerned about links to premature births and stillbirths, while outdoor workers, children and older people face particular risks. Joy Shumake-Guillemot, of WMO, explained to UN News how meteorologists and health professionals are working together to reduce some of those risks. Through a joint initiative with WHO, climate information is being brought into public health planning. A forecast of dangerously high temperatures, for example, can help hospitals prepare for more patients, while rainfall and seasonal predictions can help health authorities anticipate outbreaks of diseases such as malaria. The main character at the center of this story is not the atmosphere. It’s not the land, the ocean or the ice. It’s us – Alan Dangour, Wellcome Trust Foundation “The weather information is very practical, it is directly relevant to the decisions being made in the health sector, but they often don't have access to it,” she said. And the potential is enormous: “From a public health perspective, almost all heat deaths are actually preventable,” Ms. Shumake-Guillemot said. Health is one of the 10 priority areas of COP31’s Action Agenda, and countries are being urged to put into practice the Belém Health Action Plan agreed at COP30. A new Antalya Initiative for Health Resilience is also being launched. Agriculture: From emissions to solutions Food and agriculture account for roughly one third of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the sector is also highly vulnerable to climate change, as rising temperatures, droughts and floods threaten crops and the livelihoods of millions of farmers. Agriculture can also be part of the solution. Cristian Barrasueta, from the World Rural Forum, told UN News that farmers are already putting some of these approaches into practice. In Fiji, for example, families are experimenting with different crop varieties and finding ways to protect their seedlings from increasingly powerful cyclones. Their role is also being discussed at COP31, where countries are reviewing the Sharm el-Sheikh programme on agriculture and food security (COP27) and deciding what comes next. For Mr. Barrasueta, the priority is ensuring that family farmers have a say in shaping climate policies and can access the funding needed to adapt. Currently, he explained, complicated procedures and multiple intermediaries make international climate finance difficult to reach, particularly for small farming organizations. The urgency is already evident in Bolivia, where a severe drought has prompted the government to declare a national emergency. More than 75,000 head of livestock have died and over 114,000 families have been affected, according to official figures. With El Niño expected to intensify in the coming months, Mr. Barrasueta warned that farmers need support now, not after years of planning and paperwork. His message echoed some of the main themes from COP31’s opening day, where UN agencies also issued stark warnings about the potential impacts of El Niño. Follow the latest developments from COP31 through our new podcast, Talk & Action, and our special daily coverage of the conference
